entries.title: Project Apex, a home screen, and tools with a face
entries.summary: The window has a name and a new shell, there is a real Home page, the news arrives once on launch instead of living in a tab, and the Tools view opens on a dashboard: clock, Steam helpers and your games in one place.

sections.title: New
items: Project Apex: the 2.9.0 shell. Sections across the top as text with an underline, the page straight on the gradient, no rail, no floating card. It is the default and you can still switch back in Settings > Interface.
A Home page. The wordmark, four doors (Quick guide, Changelog, Legal notice, Discord), the community card and a Jump back in strip of whatever you played last.

Apex Tools. The Tools view is one page in three columns: Import, a live clock, and App id of Steam with Add, Restart Steam and SteamDB. Under them sits the shelf of games LuaTools has applied to this account, with Recent / A-Z, search and Reload covers.

LuaTools, read side. Apex opens Steam's per-user stplug-in folder, parses every .lua and .acf it finds, and lists the app ids and depots each one targets. A file you drop on the import box is inspected and shown with its app id, its title when Apex knows it, and a Store page / Track in Apex choice. Removing a plugin file is an uninstall, and nothing in Apex writes a script, a manifest or an unlock into Steam.
Last news. The gaming feed opens over the home screen once per launch, with a hero story and the next four, and closes with Esc or the X.

sections.title: Changed
items: The News tab is gone. The same feed now appears where it is useful - at startup - and every story still opens on news.instant-gaming.com.
The Bypass catalogue leads with a centred row of publisher marks and a denser cover grid, instead of a list of rows.

Those tiles now carry the publishers' real marks - Ubisoft, EA, Rockstar, PlayStation, Steam, Epic and GOG - in their own colours (Simple Icons' CC0 paths). Denuvo, Xbox, Nintendo and the catch-all keep drawn glyphs.

Bypass has banners: a wide featured strip for the first title on the shelf, and every card now leads with the game's 16:9 Steam art instead of a text placeholder. Missing art falls back to the drawn banner.
The corner credit reads Created by ♥ sexykudasai - v2.9.0.
Settings > Interface picks the shell separately from the theme, so either palette can be worn with either layout.
The Lightning Tools page is Apex Tools. The fix catalogues are the tabs behind it.
Jump back in is quick launch: a cover on Home starts the game, with a play mark on hover, instead of opening its page.
The title bar is text only - PROJECT heavy, APEX light, no flame mark.
itch.io works out of the box. A key bundled with the build is used until you paste your own in Settings; your key always wins, and the bundled one is never shown in the window.
Discord Rich Presence runs on Apex's own Discord application. The application id is fixed in the app, invisible in Settings and not editable.
App id of Steam adds the title to your Apex library (or opens its store page when Apex does not know it). Steam itself is never touched.

Install in Steam hands the typed app id to the Steam client (steam://install). Steam decides what to do with it: a title the account owns installs, anything else opens its store page. Apex still writes nothing into Steam, and LuaTools is not bundled or downloaded by the launcher.

The first tab of Apex Tools is App IDs, not LuaTools. It reads Steam app ids and the stplug-in folder; naming it after the third-party client made it look like Apex ships that client. The intro copy says the same thing now.

A title can show in Steam's library from an app-id file and still refuse to download. Steam needs a licence for the account and depot manifests to fetch; without them the tile stays at update required. Apex does not seed manifests or fetch depot content, so it cannot turn that tile into a download.

sections.title: Fixed
items: An emulator with no download page no longer throws an invalid-URL error at boot when its update check comes back empty.
Publisher tiles with no glyph fall back to their initials instead of an empty box.
The active catalogue tab uses the theme accent, not the old blue gradient.
Long headlines in the startup panel stay on two lines, so the row of cards keeps one height.

entries.title: A locked door, EA games, emulators, and a way to reach me
entries.summary: Sign-in now talks to the real Apex account server and cannot be pointed anywhere else, your EA App games are finally detected, there is a whole Emulators view, Big Picture finally covers every section, the Store stopped stuttering while you type, and there is a Contact page.

sections.title: New
items: An Emulators view. Apex finds the emulators you already have installed, walks your ROM folders, sorts what it finds onto a shelf per console and launches a title straight into the right emulator.
A panel of genuinely free ROM sources - archive.org public-domain sets, itch.io freeware, homebrew hubs, ScummVM and OpenTTD - so the shelf only ever points at things that are free to get.
Big Picture now reaches everything: Emulators, Gallery and Tools are browsable shelves, and Profile and Contact open as full pages, so no section of the launcher needs a mouse.
Contact page: my Discord and Telegram, one click to copy or open.
A live clock in the top right corner.
EA App, Ubisoft Connect and Battle.net titles now carry their own store badge.
A small build stamp in the corner of the window, so you always know exactly which build you are running.

sections.title: Fixed
items: EA App and Origin games are detected properly. The old probe only read registry keys the modern EA App never writes, so those titles were invisible to Apex.
Game names from the registry keep their real characters. The trademark sign in a title was being silently rewritten to a letter T.

sections.title: Improved
items: The Store no longer rebuilds every card on every keystroke, which is where the stutter while searching came from.
Big Picture fits eleven sections without squeezing the labels, and the shelf fades where there is more of it to the right.
The controller on-screen keyboard and the live search keep working exactly as before; only the wasted work is gone.

sections.title: Changed
items: The account server is compiled into the build. The sign-in screen has no server field and Settings shows the address read-only, so nobody can point the launcher at a different backend.

entries.title: Overlay, achievements and a proper goodbye
entries.summary: Performance overlay on F8, screenshots on F2, achievements you can actually earn, and an uninstall that deletes the files instead of hiding them.

sections.title: New
items: Uninstall or remove: deleting a game now really deletes it, and says exactly which folders and how much space first.
Performance overlay: F8 floats a click-through panel over any game with real CPU, GPU and RAM readings.
Screenshots: F2 grabs the screen, saves a PNG and files it in a gallery you can browse and prune.
Achievements: Apex awards its own from what you actually do, with a Steam-style toast, and can pull your real Steam achievements with your own Web API key.
What's new: a changelog bundled with the app, shown once each time it updates.

sections.title: Improved
items: The controller on-screen keyboard opens for every search box and has a button of its own.
Archive extraction reports a live percentage, so a long unrar no longer looks frozen.

sections.title: Notes
items: The overlay measures what it can honestly measure. A true in-game frame rate needs a graphics hook, so the panel labels its frame timing as the desktop's present rate and never claims to be the game's own.

entries.title: Nexus and the download engine
entries.summary: A new catalogue alongside a real multi-provider download pipeline.

sections.title: New
items: Nexus: search a second catalogue, with mirrors resolved per provider and automatic failover.
Tools: the Bypass, OnlineFix and SteamLess panels, with their catalogues refreshed from GitHub.
Downloads that start from the launcher with no window, no tab and no site to click through.
